speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In 1973, then-Minister for Finance Hon Sui Sen emphasised that “our industrialisation can best be brought about through broadening our international connections and through an unrelenting striving for quality in all aspects of our activities… our own national enterprises, too, must make a greater contribution to our future industrial development.” Those wise words from 45 years ago remain as relevant today.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We have been resolute through the decades in our commitment to developing our enterprises, but our approach has evolved in tandem with our economy, the needs of industry and the external environment.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In our formative years, we established the Department of Trade under the Ministry of Trade and Industry, which in 1983 became the Trade Development Board.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We also formed the National Productivity Board in 1972 which, together with the Singapore Institute of Standards and Industrial Research (SISIR), became the Productivity and Standards Board (PSB) in 1996.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These agencies subsequently became IE Singapore and SPRING Singapore in 2002.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Collectively, IE Singapore, SPRING Singapore and their predecessor agencies have rendered consistent and strong support to the growth of Singapore enterprises in trade, internationalisation and capability development.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: About 36,000 of these companies were small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Over the years, IE and SPRING Singapore have developed deep expertise and extensive networks in support of their mission.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: However, there have been significant changes in the nature and pace of change in the global economy which have profound implications for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: First, the weight of global growth is shifting to Asia, which is projected to grow at about 5.8% in 2018, compared to 2.1% in advanced economies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our companies have recognised that the rise of Asia is a major opportunity to internationalise quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Overseas expansion ranks among the top five business priorities for SMEs, and 60% of participants in the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s (SCCCI's) Annual Business Survey had plans to internationalise over the next three years.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, the message has been hoisted in and it is being acted upon.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Second, the advent of e-commerce and digital technology is making it easier than ever before to access overseas markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Scaling up and growing beyond our borders is now possible at a much earlier stage in an enterprise’s evolution and, indeed, has become even more important to success.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Productivity and innovation must be the basis for the sustained growth of our businesses, especially when dealing with pervasive disruptive technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The confluence of these trends necessitates a different approach towards the development of our enterprises and their ability to seize the opportunities around us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In this new environment, companies need to integrate capability-building, innovation and internationalisation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These areas of pursuit are deeply intertwined and they reinforce one another.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: A company must innovate and deepen its capabilities if it is to successfully expand into overseas markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But, equally, venturing overseas will itself create the scale and the impetus and opportunity for businesses to gain new capabilities and expertise.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As highlighted by the Committee on the Future Economy, Singapore enterprises must adapt equally to these changes, and quickly, to remain competitive.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our economic agencies must also respond to this dynamic environment and hone their efforts to support enterprise development and internationalisation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, it is necessary and timely to merge the functions and operations of IE and SPRING Singapore to form Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This merger also underscores the Government’s commitment to review its programmes and, when necessary, restructure its agencies, in its continuing effort to support the growth of our businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Enterprise Singapore will adopt an enterprise-centric approach, providing differentiated programmes and support according to a company’s stage of growth, the industry within which it operates and its overseas markets of interest.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To achieve this, Enterprise Singapore will deepen its knowledge of industries’ and companies’ needs, expand its partnerships and networks in Singapore as well as overseas, and develop a cohesive suite of programmes to enable enterprise growth.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Enterprise Singapore will work with a broad spectrum of businesses, from startups to scale-ups to SMEs, and be the single point of contact for Singapore-based enterprises which are committed to growth.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Enterprise Singapore will support upgrading, innovation and business model transformation to capture new revenue streams, promote digitalisation, automation and adoption of new technologies to improve productivity and overcome resource constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It will facilitate expansion into overseas markets and business diversification and strengthen enterprises’ leadership and management capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Enterprise Singapore’s mission is central to Singapore’s long-term economic strategy, especially as we enter the next phase of our economic growth.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The scope of its work is wide and the scale can be daunting, given the large number of enterprises that we are dealing with.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To succeed, it is important that Enterprise Singapore work closely with private and public sector partners and have their full support.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It will also work closely with other Government agencies to promote public-private partnerships, as well as collaboration between multinational corporations (MNCs), large local enterprises (LLEs), SMEs and startups to enhance the collective competitiveness of our industries.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I want to cite the precision engineering sector as an example of how such partnerships can be valuable.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Economic Development Board (EDB), SPRING Singapore, SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) and Workforce Singapore (WSG) worked with the Singapore Precision Engineering and Technology Association (SPETA) to enhance the industry's manpower capabilities through programmes, such as the Skills Framework for Precision Engineering.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: IE worked with SPRING Singapore and a group of precision engineering SMEs to form the Singapore Manufacturing Innovation Centre (SMIC) in Guangzhou Knowledge City, a platform that helps our SMEs venture into a major international market and allows them to co-create innovative technology solutions with Chinese enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: SPETA worked with IE and SPRING Singapore to set up a group of industry veterans to advise SMEs on business and technology strategies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, by leveraging each other's strengths, public agencies and TACs can help our companies compete internationally.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The formation of Enterprise Singapore will give greater impetus to such partnerships.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The agency will continue this important work, which is key to promoting innovation and strengthening the capabilities and competitiveness of our companies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Enterprise Singapore will also build on IE's efforts to promote the export of goods and services and establish Singapore as Asia's foremost trading hub by anchoring new players in Singapore to grow a strong domestic trade network.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This includes strengthening Singapore's trade infrastructure in areas of product development and liquidity-building initiatives for sectors, such as commodity derivatives.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This means ensuring that the competencies, knowledge, experience and networks developed by IE and SPRING Singapore are preserved.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Also, that Enterprise Singapore will retain and build on the relationships that IE and SPRING Singapore have developed with enterprises and partners both here in Singapore and overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And that current programmes and schemes, such as the Local Enterprise and Association Development (LEAD) scheme, continue to be administered even as they are streamlined and new programmes developed to better support enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Enterprise Singapore will undertake these in a manner that will minimise disruption and maximise opportunities for enterprises and their staff.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Parts 1 and 2 of the Bill provide for the key concepts used in the Bill and to establish Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Part 2 also sets out Enterprise Singapore's functions and powers, which are drawn and streamlined from existing provisions in the SPRING Singapore and IE Board Acts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These cover the enterprise development, internationalisation, wholesale and commodity trading, and productivity, innovation and standards functions that SPRING Singapore and IE currently perform.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The consumer protection fair trading function has been excluded in view of the transfer to CCCS.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Parts 3 to 6 cover matters regarding the appointment of Enterprise Singapore's Board members and their decision-making procedures, Enterprise Singapore's employees and its financial provisions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Relevant provisions have been aligned and streamlined with the Public Service (Governance) Act, which was passed in Parliament on 8 January this year.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Part 7 of the Bill sets out the administration and enforcement powers of Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In particular, this Part will allow Enterprise Singapore to request and verify information in relation to its incentive schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It will also protect against improper use of certification and accreditation marks that are administered by Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These provisions will facilitate the effective administration of incentives and grants, and better support Enterprise Singapore in its role as the national standards and accreditation body.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Parts 8 and 9 contain provisions that transfer the relevant undertakings and personnel to Enterprise Singapore, to repeal the IE and SPRING Singapore Board Acts, and provide for saving and transitional arrangements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is so true both in substance and in the spirit of it.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to restructure to stay relevant and to up the game, and this applies to all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This merger signalled to businesses that we need to look beyond our small and near-saturated domestic market to seek new growth frontiers overseas so as to sustain economic growth and job creations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Otherwise, we run the risk of a stagnant economy and may even decline as regional competitors step up and eat our lunches.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As more companies trade, service and venture overseas, it does not make good sense to have more than one agency serving the same enterprise, where the overlapping coverage can actually add more administrative work for companies and it is also a case of sub-optimal utilisation of resources.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Internationalisation requires capabilities building, and both are actually inseparable and intertwined when companies expand into overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, the need for an integrated and a more lifecycle approach to help companies grow and build capabilities, developing competitive advantages that can help sell their products and services to the consumers of the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over the years, SPRING Singapore and IE Singapore have done a good job helping businesses, each engaging and assisting tens of thousands of enterprises per year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my interactions with businesses, I do hear good feedback and accolades from companies on the work done by SPRING Singapore and IE Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the other hand, I have also heard comments from businesses that they would prefer to deal with one single agency, one point of contact, for Government-related support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, we all buy in to the merger.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, how can the new Enterprise Singapore do a better job helping businesses to grow?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The merger presents a timely opportunity to fundamentally restructure the merged organisation and reconfigure its functionalities to meet both the present and future needs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Presently, SPRING Singapore, with its multiple SME Centres, and IE Singapore with its overseas Singapore Centres in major cities, have been a very useful first stop or touchpoint for businesses seeking help.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Coupled with its sectoral coverage, they have been able to maximise their outreach, especially to SMEs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope that the locations and sectoral coverage will continue under the new Statutory Board and grow further as many companies continue to need assistance and support in this next phase where we deepen restructuring.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Soon after the merger was announced last year, a concerned business executive asked me whether, for the post-merger, will there be rationalisation and reduction of total headcount for the combined entity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My answer to him was that I hope not.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, we should seek efficiency and streamline any duplications and unnecessary workflows but I believe the motivation and purpose of the merger is not about reducing headcount and to cut costs but rather to be more effective in assisting companies by way of harnessing the combined and now more integrated resources of the two entities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With more extensive use of technology and various platforms, including through the TACs and Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), Enterprise Singapore should aim to further expand its outreach to businesses, including reaching out to the newer SMEs and micro enterprises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The new Statutory Board should also continue its work to simplify ways for businesses to tap on the various support schemes, such as using platforms like the Business Grant Portal (BGP).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There should also be, in parallel, a regular closing of the loop on the utilised schemes to ascertain their effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Unlike attracting MNCs which bring along their capabilities and cutting-edge technology when they invest in Singapore, developing local capabilities of home-bred companies can be a very formidable task.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But in reality, we also know that the ITMs are essentially driven by one of the key economic agencies, such as Enterprise Singapore, going forward, which are like the workhorse facilitating the transformations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, it is critical to the success of ITMs that economic agencies like Enterprise Singapore have the deep industry knowledge, a good ground sense of the prevailing competitive landscape, a good knowledge of the sectoral strengths and gaps as well as enough business acumen to design meaningful policies and schemes to incentivise and help capability buildup.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: All these are a tall order to expect from a Government agency, staffed by career Public Service officers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fortunately for Singapore, economic development has always been our foremost priority.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our system of Government and its policies have always been pro-business and pro-growth, and officers are frequently rotated to economic-oriented Ministries and Statutory Boards to gain exposure and experience in economic development.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nevertheless, to diversify its bench strength and to add to its organisational versatility, Enterprise Singapore should also look to continually recruit and induct officers from the private sector with relevant industry and international business experiences.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One functionality that the new Enterprise Singapore can step up is in the area of helping SMEs build their brands and promotion overseas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some SMEs may be too caught up in developing their product capabilities and may not have the resource or sufficient know-how to more effectively sell and brand their products in overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As companies seek opportunities beyond the traditional developed markets to newer emerging markets with unfamiliar business environment, the availability of shared brand-building and marketing expertise for specific external markets will be of good help to SMEs and to speed up market penetration.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I suggest that the new Statutory Board have a dedicated unit to assist companies in their brand building and product promotion in overseas markets, especially in the ASEAN and South Asian markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my interactions with businesses, most recently with the contract manufacturing sector, finance-related issues continued to affect SMEs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Most of the issues relate to delays in payments from customers, although high interest rates for bank loans and tighter suppliers’ credit are also cited among the business issues faced.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I know that there are various useful SME financing schemes available to assist enterprises to finance their businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From the survey, I believe the other help that SMEs need is to improve their financial management capabilities, such as cash management and credit management, for both their customers and suppliers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As more businesses internationalise, such cash and credit management become more complex when they are cross-border.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It requires a deeper understanding of the in-country business practices and its legal framework.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should help SMEs shorten the learning curve and minimise the chances of them paying the "tuition fee" in unfamiliar territories.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, Enterprise Singapore and the TACs can help pool and share experiences from businesses which are already overseas and learn from one another's practices and experiences.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, from the survey, it is encouraging to note that more SMEs are making fresh investments in technology and innovation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And importantly, more are also getting revenue gains from their technology investments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Increasingly, data technology is seen as a critical enabler for business successes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For smaller enterprises, to build their own data mining and analytical capabilities may not be economical.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Enterprise Singapore can also help in this regard, for example, as a source of data aggregator on industry trends and insights and harnessing on information already collected by other Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Specialised functionality within the new Statutory Board can be set up to extract and manage data, distilling them into sufficient sectoral granularity that will be of help and usefulness to various business sectors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We could start with the building up of deep data resources for sectors of the 23 ITMs that are already launched.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In an increasingly fast-changing business landscape, the enlarged organisation would need to gear up its quick-response ability to keep up with changing business needs, in addition to developing its breadth and depth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The new operating framework would also require sufficient empowerment to officers at the various levels to carry out their mission of transforming the economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not easy by any means, but we have high confidence in the new chairman-designate Mr Peter Ong and the new Chief Executive Officer (CEO)-designate Mr Png Cheong Boon.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must not underestimate the changes that businesses, both large and small, face with the technological advances we are witnessing today.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Growing connectivity has led to the defining of a new economy with evolving business models, how products and services are delivered and consumed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There is also a trend of sharing and partnerships.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Even in the area of manpower, employment models are changing with access to different sources of skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There is a greater use of independent and freelance workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As Finance Minister Heng Swee Keat recently said, global and technological changes are causing the blurring of industry boundaries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He stressed the importance to consider "the convergence of sectors".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There will be an increasing need for Enterprise Singapore to partner across several agencies to deliver the appropriate help to businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: SPRING Singapore and IE Singapore are already connecting and enabling the sharing amongst businesses to improve productivity and helping them internationalise.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The food manufacturing industry is one good example of this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With digitalisation and the new economy, I see an opportunity for the new Enterprise Singapore to play an even bigger and somewhat different role in connecting businesses to build capability, grow and go global.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As the Minister had shared in his speech earlier, the approach has to evolve in tandem with the change the industry is facing and also with the needs of businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Last week, in a pre-Budget dialogue that I had with SMEs, an SME leader shared the challenges she is facing with regard to addressing some of her customer needs because of her limited delivery capability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: She was looking at how she could tap the excess capacity of other small businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There was another business leader in the room and she quickly said that she had excess capacity in her off-peak periods and would be able to support this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I know this is a very simple example but I hope it demonstrates the need and potential for an ecosystem that connects companies for greater effectiveness and efficiencies to leverage their capabilities and capacities locally and even overseas.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And providing them also relevant information and insights.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Yes, you could say that businesses could do this themselves but this peer-to-peer approach may not be as effective, especially in a world where businesses need to move faster and be a lot more responsive to the market.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For ecosystems to cooperate effectively, you need support to enable efficient collaboration and information sharing both within and amongst businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Enterprise Singapore can and should play that role both for SMEs and larger businesses albeit how the support is structured will differ.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not about providing more infrastructure or more grants but rather connecting and enabling businesses to collaborate effectively for joint success.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As the Minister so rightly put it, building business capability, innovating and internationalisation are so much more intertwined now.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There also could be more done across different industries, and not just within industries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This brings me to my final and related point.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because what a business is, who your employees are, where your resources come from will really differ as we move forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a move may eliminate any potential interagency overlap or rivalries and reduce confusion and time on the part of enterprises seeking Government support.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, integrating all functions relating to fair trade under the new CCCS would have the same streamlining and rationalising effect.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, this is a step in the right direction and I do not oppose this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The work of supporting local enterprise is critical, so as to grow a third pillar to drive value creation and job creation for our economy, alongside the pillars of MNCs and Government-linked entities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before I do so, I declare that I am the CEO of a research consultancy that works with a wide spectrum of end-clients, including some SMEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The term "SME" is a convenient shorthand which we all use.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, there are often big differences between the S and the M.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Aside from just size, there are differences in terms of the mindset of the entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some SMEs are more focused on stability, have modest ambitions and may not want to become the next Facebook.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But others are more focused on growth and should be encouraged and supported to become dynamic job creation and value creation engines for our economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For those enterprises which may be small or mid-sized and not in a hurry to grow radically, largely domestically-oriented and/or are more focused on stability rather than growth, there is a case for supporting such enterprises with challenges like productivity, internationalisation and business succession planning, so as to maintain jobs and grow wages.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The approach taken to support these SMEs could be more oriented towards programme administration.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But on top of that, some of those enterprises could be nudged into using incentive schemes towards sunrise sectors within their own broad industry or in adjacent industries where they have core competencies that can be leveraged.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, there are enterprises that have the potential to become regional or global champions, those with the ambition, drive and ability to become engines for job creation and value creation for our economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These would need support in a much more open-ended way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The appropriate approach to support such enterprises would be to provide more aggressive support in a more holistic, responsive and creative way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such enterprises may need support in terms of human capital, recruiting management and expert talent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They may need support to obtain financing where, at some stages of growth, some SMEs continue to experience an inability to raise sufficient financing from capital markets, venture capitalists (VCs) or banks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And they would need support in terms of internationalisation and overseas market penetration, or even foreign direct investment to locate parts of their global business supply chain abroad while keeping critical headquarters and other functions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The optimal approach for such enterprises would perhaps involve tapping on whole-of-Government resources to enable them to resolve problems in their overseas operations or to introduce them to sources of funding or potential partners, to cite two examples.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The different approaches that are called for may require separate divisions and separate operating styles in those divisions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, and to take this a little further, does the Government try to arrange a single account manager for each company for Government support, across all agencies?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That account manager could reside in different agencies, for example, the Singapore Tourism Board (STB) for tourism-related companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Anecdotally, it would appear that some companies sometimes may not be completely clear about whether there is a single Government account manager currently along these lines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And how will this differentiation be conveyed to the companies that these agencies serve?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, I trust that one area the new Enterprise Singapore will actively look into is how to catalyse links between Singapore companies when they operate in international markets.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do see such links between some companies from foreign countries when they move abroad, whereby such companies cluster into specific areas or even buildings and business centres, share learnings and networks, and thus, shorten the learning curve and lessen the risk for one another.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is especially important in difficult markets, like Africa, which is probably the next and last frontier in emerging market region.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would like know what Enterprise Singapore plans to do on this issue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The consolidation of most state support to local enterprises under one roof has the potential to create a powerful one-stop shop to support our local enterprises in ways that are appropriate to their entrepreneurial trajectory for maximum benefit to our economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Local enterprises need to be a strong third pillar of our economy alongside MNCs and Government-linked companies (GLCs).

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many were pleased that they could look forward to holistic support from one organisation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill has proposed several thoughtful measures that will smoothen the merger process, thus giving reassurance to businesses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This will ensure that any fraudulent claims can be identified and disallowed before the merger takes place, as not doing so could complicate matters.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It would be difficult to trace the fraud after the merger, or determine which party is responsible.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This shows the dedication of both Boards in safeguarding public funds.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When the merger was first announced, some SMEs expressed concern.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This arose among those who were in the midst of making significant plans and exploring options for their business, and they realised that by the time they are to submit their grant application, both Boards would be caught up in the merger transition.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Improving transparency of the process also provides assurances to these SMEs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Previously, officers from SPRING Singapore would usually conduct one or two follow-up sessions after businesses have implemented the acquired systems and upgrades.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And if no anomaly is detected during the follow-up sessions, it is considered case-closed and the businesses are then left to fend for themselves.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe the frequency of officers following up with the companies could be looked into to ensure that the implemented system is, indeed, aiding the company’s growth and progression as initially projected.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the company is still experiencing trouble in achieving that progression within a stipulated timeframe, then there should be guidelines in place to extend further assistance to the company.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As the time taken for companies to adapt to the new systems would differ due to many factors, the amount and type of assistance required would vary.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I think Enterprise Singapore would want to look carefully into the grant applications to ensure that the submissions for upgrades are justifiable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The most expensive is not always the best but, for some applicants, they may adopt this mantra.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The key to achieving greater effectiveness is to tailor solutions and assistance schemes to each company.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Every company faces unique challenges and the differences in the challenges would vary even more greatly across different industries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps a small panel of consultants or experts could be appointed to conduct in-depth industry analyses and identify the common problems faced by these individual industries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Adopt a proactive approach to engage companies and encourage them to adopt solutions based on the gaps identified by the experts.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Appoint solution providers who have been pre-vetted for suitability, to assist with the implementation of solutions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Pre-vet the cost of implementation and negotiate better pricing where possible to ensure that the grants can help companies to achieve even more.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If shortage of manpower is a concern, freelancing consultants, auditors and other professionals can be engaged to help perform the relevant follow-ups to ensure that each implementation achieves the desired results.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They hope that the pooling of resources will support SMEs in their aspirations to make their mark in the increasingly competitive business world.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps through the strengthening of collaborations with the various industry partners, there could be more missions to bring our SMEs for overseas exposure to explore opportunities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   I hope the merger of IE Singapore and SPRING Singapore can consolidate the resources and provide more support for local companies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: According to my knowledge, after a company has implemented certain improvement measures, Government officers would usually conduct one or two follow-up sessions to make sure that everything goes well.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If no anomaly is detected, it is considered case closed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that, in future, the Government can follow up more closely to make sure that improvement measures have, indeed, worked.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When companies apply for grants, the Government should not just hand out the grants.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, it should have a set of standards to make sure that the planned improvement measures are truly beneficial.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government should check on the companies more often on things like whether they are providing better services and prices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government can also work with experts and auditors to craft and implement such standards.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is a clear reflection of the Government’s commitment to help companies achieve success.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With further improvements, I believe that many more businesses will benefit substantially from this new Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This shows that while the Government urges industries and businesses to transform, it is also actively playing a leading role.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I recall that in 2009, SCCCI proposed eight recommendations to the Economic Strategies Committee on behalf of the business community.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: One of the recommendations was to set up a Statutory Board to provide one-stop services for enterprise development, streamline its processes so that companies do not have to go back and forth among the various Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We applaud the Government for heeding the recommendations of the business community and certainly look forward to this new agency.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This ranking showed us that in terms of transformation and innovation, there is still a lot of room for our local enterprises to improve.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, SMEs are stepping up their transformation process and working hard to keep abreast of national economic growth.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the new economic environment, the Government is adjusting its structure by setting up a dedicated agency to help develop local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, the newly set up Enterprise Singapore Board will have a heavy responsibility and a long road ahead.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Previously, IE Singapore and SPRING Singapore helped local enterprises via two different routes.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: While IE Singapore’s mission was to lead larger local enterprises in expanding overseas, SPRING Singapore was responsible for helping SMEs improve their capability.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses are now concerned about how the new agency would operate after 1 April.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: How do our businesses deal with this new agency?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: What kind of new experiences will they have?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I take this opportunity to share some views of the business community.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: How would the new agency take care of different industries and the needs of enterprises of different sizes?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Would they be an important part of the agency’s customers?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: How would MTI set key performance indicators (KPIs) for the officers?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In assessing their work performance, would they be evaluated based on the economic value-add of the industry under their care, or the size and number of companies they have helped?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Or would it be based on other performance indicators?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, when companies which fall within the ITMs and those from non-ITM sectors approach the new agency for assistance, will they be given different priorities?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: For companies with the intention to upgrade but are not from the ITM sectors, will they be treated differently from those from the key industries?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Fourthly, will the plethora of Government assistance schemes continue to exist, or will they be streamlined and reclassified according to the needs of enterprises at different stages of their development?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from these, businesses also hope that the new agency could continue to work closely with EDB.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As we embark on transforming our economy via our ITMs, a key pillar of transformation lies in the internationalisation of our enterprises.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Given the small domestic market in Singapore, internationalisation is the key engine of growth and transformation for Singapore companies and our economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This will give our efforts to transform our economy a concerted push forward.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the past, an SME would have to go to SPRING Singapore to address their capability development needs and then to IE Singapore if they needed support in internationalising their business.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The SME would have to submit documents to both agencies and maintain relations with officers from each agency.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the merger, the SME need only approach Enterprise Singapore for support for both their capability development and internationalisation needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This will not only reduce the administrative burden on the SME but also allow the officer-in-charge to have a more holistic overview of the strategic direction and growth trajectory of the SME to better enable the provision of more efficient and effective support as the SME evolves.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, I have some questions on the details of this consolidation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, in view of the merger, staff from both SPRING Singapore and IE Singapore will have to take on new roles and expanded job scopes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: SPRING Singapore has about 500 employees while IE Singapore has about 450.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The staff in Enterprise Singapore must be familiar with both the mandates, schemes and grants of SPRING Singapore and IE Singapore in order to provide SMEs with the one-stop advisory and support envisioned.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How are staff being prepared for this expanded job scope?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Would there be any support provided to them during this transitioning period?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On a related note, CCS will be taking over SPRING Singapore’s oversight of consumer protection.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Will existing staff in SPRING Singapore in charge of this area of work be transferred to CCS or will staff at CCS be taking on these new responsibilities?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If so, how are the staff at CCS being prepared for this expanded job scope?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, in every merger, the challenge lies in integrating the cultures of the merging organisations and co-creating the new culture of the merged organisation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What efforts are being undertaken to smoothen this transitional phase for the employees of Enterprise Singapore?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, how will SMEs which are currently being supported by SPRING Singapore and/or IE Singapore be affected by the consolidation?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Will these SMEs be assigned with new staff due to the consolidation?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, with the consolidation of SPRING Singapore and IE Singapore, will there be a streamlining of grants and schemes currently offered by the two sector agencies?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are many grants and schemes offered by both SPRING Singapore and IE Singapore respectively and, currently, SMEs already require assistance in identifying which grants and schemes are more suitable for them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Given that Enterprise Singapore will be a one-stop support for SMEs, it may be timely to review the grants and schemes available and assess if it would be useful to tier them to cater to the different developmental needs and stages of the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Lastly, with the coming together of SPRING Singapore and IE Singapore, Enterprise Singapore will be connected to a larger pool of SMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Are there plans to leverage this expanded network of SMEs to build stronger interlinks within our SME community?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The success stories of these SMEs can serve as guides for smaller SMEs to emulate.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Through this network, smaller SMEs can also build business links with the larger SMEs to create mutual business value by leveraging each other’s strengths and value propositions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I also urge Enterprise Singapore to work closely with our Labour Movement’s U SME to address the issues and challenges faced by our SMEs and make every SME workplace a better workplace, every SME job a better job, and every SME worker a better worker.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Regarding the merger of the two agencies, I have three questions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Their job scope may change or expand, and the corporate culture may also be different.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What kind of support will they receive so as to build a new corporate culture?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Are there measures to ensure a smooth transition?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Thirdly, the economic network will be expanded after the merger.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is my hope that more SMEs will benefit, receive one-stop services, improve their productivity and internationalise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But many SMEs continue to face many challenges.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: SME owners know that they have to respond swiftly or risk being irrelevant.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These changes are not just unique to certain companies; they are prevalent across industries.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, many businesses want closer collaboration within the industry and for the Government to be more involved.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, we set up coordination bodies like the National Productivity Council and the Future Economy Committee.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, I am very concerned about our SMEs, especially the micro-SMEs, as they need to change fast.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The disruptive future we have been talking about is happening now.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Despite all these efforts, we have yet to see deep participation of many SMEs and micro-SMEs in the ITMs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We need to understand why this may be so.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: From my understanding, I think there are two common factors that help industries be successful in following through the transformation spelt out in their respective ITMs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Driving and catalysing industry transformation will be a very important part of Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I would like to propose three points for Enterprise Singapore’s consideration.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The accounting and law sectors are prime examples of how TACs have been professionalised.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For one, they are staffed by relevant industry professionals who then bring with them the domain expertise in industry promotion or transformational work.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Having people with the relevant knowledge and experience in TACs also means that they can help the TACs develop industry code of conduct, standards, benchmarking and development programmes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There is great value in getting each TAC to be staffed by people of their respective industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Effective TACs are not just limited to firms practising professional services.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: SBF thus has the capital, legitimacy and professionals who have the clout to fulfil their mandate to help the larger companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond the general business chambers, the real leadership and drive for ITM transformation must come from the specific trade associations, which have a more intimate knowledge of the industry and experience.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Thus, we can look to get the trade associations to have greater ownership.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can also see how we can better resource these associations and industry bodies to have relevant professionals so that they can provide effective leadership.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This can come through mandatory participation and affordable membership fees.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: That brings me to my second point ‒ the role of the SME Centres.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It will be difficult to ensure that every sector has an effective TAC.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Within any sector, there are also many smaller industries.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, there is scope for SME Centres to play a dual role, which is to drive the ITMs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They can drive ITMs by encouraging geographical or industry collaborations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, the SME Centres can provide the industries within the same location with the advantage of the use of common facilities, shared services and shared marketing resources.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This will especially help the smaller companies and industries.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The SME Centres can also develop industry-specific knowledge by hiring existing staff with relevant knowledge.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Alternatively, Enterprise Singapore can also consider co-opting staff, preferably with industry experience, to an SME Centre so that the SME Centre can be a focal point to help specific industry ITMs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: My last point is to tap on additional media channels.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While we are doing all that, there is still a danger of some companies falling through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After all, we cannot force some companies to come up to the SME Centre if they are not aware of the initiatives to drive the transformation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our Singapore SME landscape is such that many of their owners may not be English-educated and may not be very familiar with many Government schemes or incentives.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While I know that agencies like SPRING Singapore have made an effort in recent years to reach out to the non-English media, there is scope to do more.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Reaching out to SMEs through Lianhe Zaobao may not be sufficient.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some of them read evening dailies, like Shin Min Daily or Wanbao.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The problem is that many of our SME leaders are not plugged into the national newspapers and simply do not have the luxury of time to flip through the newspapers every day.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, we should encourage and explore all forms of media communication, including radio and the media from the Malay and Tamil languages.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We could discuss on industry-specific transformation on these news channels and do so in the language of the everyday Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, we can have a programme talking about the fate of the prata makers, something that will gel with the everyday Singaporean and make people aware of the issues.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This is important because many SME owners and workers, especially from micro-SMEs, are everyday Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One might wonder whether it is possible to capture the imagination of everyday Singaporeans, especially on this seemingly technical subject of industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When we talk about industry 4.0, technical terms get thrown around liberally.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The feedback from the business community, including food manufacturers, is very positive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They generally see greater efficiency in this new body where they do not have to shuttle and interface with two agencies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would facilitate the provision of more holistic support for enterprises to succeed in both domestic and overseas markets and better respond to the challenges presented in these markets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as with all mergers, it is to rise to concerns about continuity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister has mentioned this in his opening speech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, I would just like to focus a bit on the details.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Having a different account manager is a concern shared by some companies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope Enterprise Singapore will do their best to retain the same account managers for business continuity and to minimise changes for the companies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Where it is not possible to retain the same account managers, I would like to ask what steps will be taken to make the transition as seamless as possible.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If a new account manager is to be deployed, frequent follow-ups would help to build relationships, create assurance and familiarity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Certainly, as long as the new manager is committed to the success and welfare of the business, his/her identity should not be of grave concern.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ultimately, there is not a single solution or even specific formulae that could apply across the board as no two enterprises are the same, and this goes even for those in the same industry.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would be more productive to craft strategies and implementation together with each enterprise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also believe SMEs, including smaller enterprises, will remain an important priority group for Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Embedding technology and digitalisation in the form-filling procedures could save a lot of time and manpower, which is valuable to SMEs with a small headcount.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, all businesses, not just SMEs, should benefit from such positive advances.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   Next, I would like to discuss some feedback and findings by the Singapore Malay Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SMCCI), which did a pre-Budget survey with the Muslim/Malay business community recently.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Among the top business concerns are rising labour and rental costs, the outlook of the global economy, and keeping up with the digitalisation trend.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For 2018, the top strategies to stay relevant include creating new products and services, entering new markets and managing operating costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are good long-term strategies and in line with IE Singapore and also SPRING Singapore’s vision to nurture successful enterprises through growth and internationalisation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe Enterprise Singapore, with its existing capabilities, resources and new focus on digitalisation, is in a good position to help them succeed with their strategies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These areas are brand building, overseas growth and technology adoption.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a positive sign that companies recognise the value of brand-building.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, having a strong brand is a prerequisite to establishing one’s presence in the overseas market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hopefully, we can have a brand that is well-received, just like, for instance, IKEA.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope Enterprise Singapore can provide more support to businesses in this area.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One solution or suggestion would be to provide more media-related grants which companies can use for their branding endeavours.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would also be ideal to create more cross-border opportunities spearheaded by Government agencies, allowing them to get more exposure and experience.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government has been partnering local firms for infrastructure and construction projects overseas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, other industries could benefit through similar partnerships.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Finally, under the ITM initiatives, the Government has been developing ITMs to address issues within the targeted industries and promote synergy across agencies that can provide support.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some sectors are quite extensive, and they may appear to not come under the ITMs for the targeted industries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, some of these SMEs are already getting assistance and support rendered by IE Singapore and SPRING Singapore to SMEs which, in essence, are part of the ITM, I believe.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But they feel that they have been left out because these efforts are not branded as ITM initiatives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I have mentioned earlier, no two organisations are the same, and not every organisation would fall under the ITM.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is evidence of the Government diversifying efforts to reach out to all parts of a sector as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These past two years have seen the economy rapidly changing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Keeping abreast with new demands, creating new products and reinventing existing ones in response to the changes are key to staying relevant.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Expanding into new markets, too, will help to open up more opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Enterprise Singapore, too, will do well to review and enhance its existing programmes and help enable local enterprises to scale to greater heights.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I wish to raise just four points for clarification and consideration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Enterprise Singapore has the mandate of supporting our enterprises in internationalising.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How does the Minister intend to respond to these findings?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The merger of SPRING Singapore and IE Singapore is a significant undertaking and Minister Iswaran has emphasised that the priority is to "ensure a smooth transition".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Assurance had been given that, in the transition period, support for SMEs will not be affected and companies can continue to apply to SPRING Singapore and IE Singapore for assistance under the existing programmes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, Enterprise Singapore is intended to streamline existing grants and provide a comprehensive suite of support from a single agency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share whether he foresees any issues in harmonising the programmes of the two agencies and what steps will be taken to reduce any inconveniences to the companies?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, I understand that SME accounts are currently managed by different agencies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Minister had highlighted efforts to streamline the account management so that there is a principal agency managing a particular relationship with a company, whether it is EDB, IE Singapore or SPRING Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister provide an update on its efforts and clarify whether Enterprise Singapore will be the principal agency managing all SME accounts, moving forward?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Also, during Question Time in September 2017, the Minister had alluded to the challenges in synthesising the missions of two organisations and the concern that one may prevail over the other.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With this focus on overseas expansion, small firms may have concerns of being neglected.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The concern was articulated by SBF's Teo Siong Seng who had voiced the concern of whether micro-enterprises, such as mom-and-pop shops in HDB estates, will be ignored in the process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Iswaran has articulated an inclusive mission to "create globally competitive Singapore enterprises" which will apply "to the whole range of enterprises from startups to scale-ups and large local enterprises".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He has emphasised that there would be "no dilution or diminution in terms of the services rendered to the wide swathe of SMEs that we have in our ecosystem".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While this is heartening to hear, can the Minister share what concrete plans it has to ensure that small and micro-enterprises are not neglected?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to highlight the need to include sustainability as part of the conversation on the growth of SMEs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the Singapore Apex Corporate Sustainability Awards in 2017, Minister Heng stated that pursuing sustainability is a "matter of survival" for businesses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As highlighted by Minister Heng, "studies show that sound sustainability standards lower a company's cost of capital and result in better operational performance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Investor demands and customer expectations are increasingly favouring sustainable businesses." Environmentally and socially sustainable growth has been receiving greater attention.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond large listed companies, we can do more to increase uptake of sustainable business practices by SMEs which are the biggest employers and contribute to the bulk of growth.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Individual efforts by SMEs to adopt sustainable practices would, collectively, represent an enormous leap forward.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To be sure, there are moves in that direction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: SMEs are part of the supply chain for listed companies and would be impacted by SGX regulations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also applaud initiatives by the Building and Construction Authority (BCA), such as increasing funding for SMEs to green their premises, providing free feasibility assessments against BCA Green Mark standards, and piloting the Behavioural Change Programme to encourage building users to adopt sustainable behaviours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another initiative is the Energy Efficiency fund, which supports businesses, including SMEs, in identifying and undertaking energy efficiency retrofits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need more of such initiatives that are specifically targeted towards SMEs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2010, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) stressed that "the prospects and strategies for a green growth economy cannot be entirely understood without taking fully into account the production, technology and management practices of SMEs".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sustainability efforts may need to be tailored to meet the needs of SMEs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, SMEs may face challenges of cost, lack of resources, lack of time, or difficulty in implementing existing sustainability indicators that are too complicated to be adopted or too high level for practical usage by small companies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Founded by Susan Chong in 2002, Greenpac is a multi-million dollar business that provides eco-friendly packaging to Fortune 500 companies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What we need is a concerted effort to push the sustainability agenda for SMEs, and Enterprise Singapore, as the leading agency for SMEs, would be well-placed for that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Changes in financing structures and supply chains and ease of doing business overseas have opened up business opportunities beyond Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is a consequent need to support our local businesses to seize such opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The new Enterprise Singapore can play such an important role.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the formation of the new agency, it should not simply be an amalgamation of two current separate approaches to helping our companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The chances to tap on overseas opportunities and best practices should influence how we help SMEs to grow.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, because many of the SMEs might not be ready for overseas expansion, how can we still ensure that these SMEs are not neglected as we help the potential winners?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They still face many pressing issues, such as improving productivity, manpower shortages and business process re-engineering.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must ensure that efforts to help them continue unabated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The new agency, with its new integrated mandate of helping businesses to grow, can also develop new ways in operationalising the ITMs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are two separate facets: one, from Singapore-to-overseas; and two, outside-and-into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, many of the ITMs were developed while the two agencies were still separate entities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How would the ITMs change now that the local-overseas nexus is much stronger?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, in the retail and food and beverage (F&B) sector where SPRING Singapore has been a major player and lead agency of the ITM, how would the merger change its approach to helping the F&B businesses?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are opportunities in getting local businesses to benefit from global supply chains and expansion opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, in the SC VivoCity project in Ho Chi Minh City, we can find familiar names, such as NTUC Fairprice via its CoopXtra venture, Breadtalk, and also Xiao Ban, which is linked to the famous Lao Ban Dou Hua.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the case of CoopXtra, the overseas venture has allowed new food supplies to be established for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that with the new agency, we can accelerate such growth and expansion of our local businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Two, from an outside-and-into Singapore perspective, there are also opportunities for the new agency to work with EDB to explore synergies in operationalising our ITMs, especially in cluster transformation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In attracting investments into Singapore, our SMEs can benefit in providing strategic partnerships and ancillary services to the MNCs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Bringing in the right MNCs can catalyse transformation in many industries, especially through horizontal competencies, such as information and communications technology (ICT) and supply chain management.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As with any merger, there is a lingering concern on the deployment of manpower.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also opens up new opportunities for us to relook at our ITMs, especially in operationalisation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I declare that I am currently the employee of a local financial institution (FI).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   By merging IE Singapore and SPRING Singapore to form Enterprise Singapore, we will be able to provide one-stop services for our enterprises.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that after the merger, Enterprise Singapore will be able to provide more comprehensive and robust coordination services to our businesses.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides helping our companies improve productivity and the quality of their products and services, Enterprise Singapore can also help them expand and explore the overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If our local enterprises hope to become even stronger in the future, they need to internationalise.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Enterprise Singapore can not only provide advisory services through its extensive network of overseas offices, but also help to link up various companies, so that they can enter overseas markets hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How many companies have defaulted and how much is the loss so far?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, you do not object to the Bill but the Party supports the Bill.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And let me now address the key points that have been raised and I will try to give some clarifications on the issues that have been brought up.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want to start by saying that, generally, the fact that the Members have supported the Bill, and I think, in general, also reflecting the mood and the opinion in the broader business community, are welcome signs because it means that we are moving in the right direction.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Many of the questions are around the details in terms of how and what we intend to do in execution, and I would endeavour to address them as much as I can.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Various Members, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Leon Perera, Mr Thomas Chua, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Desmond Choo, have asked whether Enterprise Singapore will, in fact, support enterprises of different sizes and from different industries.
